$description:
These design tokens apply to all tools. Layer 1 defines primitive color scales. Layer 2 defines semantic roles. The generators in theme/generate.clj convert the semantic tokens to tool configuration files. Tools do not read this file directly.

The scales use OKLCH and a perceptual L* sequence. Smaller increments at the light end give background tints more resolution. Each scale has one hue and a shared chroma limit of approximately 0.045 for steps 300–700. This limit gives the accents equal chroma.

Steps 100/200 use three background contrast levels: approximately 1.13:1, 1.30:1, and 1.55:1. These ratios compare the tints with the base background. The lightness sequence does not change with the chroma level. The tints distinguish states across displays, including displays without calibration. Their chroma is approximately 0.011–0.017 across hues.

The design uses one neutral background, dark text at approximately 8:1, and accents with low chroma. Accent step 600 has approximately 4.9:1 contrast. Lightness differences distinguish roles that previously used hue differences. See primitive.$description for the two chroma ranges.

primitive.$description:
Layer 1 defines color scales from step 50 (lightest) to step 900 (darkest). Each scale uses a fixed hue and a perceptual L* sequence with smaller increments at the light end.

Steps 50–200 are background tints with chroma approximately 0.006–0.017. Steps 300–700 use chroma approximately 0.045. Lightness, not chroma, distinguishes the roles in this second range. Step 300 has L≈0.82 and emphasizes selections, active searches, and changed words. Steps 600–700 are foreground colors with contrast approximately 4.8–6.1:1 against the base background.

Step N has the same lightness in the gray scale and the hue scales. The shared sequence gives the same contrast for each step. Step 300 has contrast approximately 1.5:1 and is not a foreground color. Its chroma matches the foreground range so emphasized backgrounds and accents have equal chroma.

The chroma increase from step 200 to step 300 is approximately 0.028. This increase separates background tints from emphasized backgrounds. The amber scale has a warmer hue at the light end than the other tints. See the amber description for that exception. Semantic tokens assign roles to these primitive values.

gray.$description: This neutral gray scale has chroma C*≈0. It supplies surfaces, borders, and text colors without a yellow tint. The selected lightness values keep the contrast relationships. Step 50 is the shared off-white background for Neovim, terminals, and Zellij.

red.$description:
This scale supplies errors, deletions, and the warm mode accent. The hue is approximately 18° (crimson). Dark colors with low chroma and a warm hue can appear brown. At 18°, the green and blue channels have approximately equal values. For example, step 600 is #7A6060 (G≈B).

This hue makes the dark steps appear maroon rather than brown. Hues of approximately 15° or less start to appear pink. The light steps appear pale rose, the usual Git deletion color. The dark steps appear dark red.

The addition and deletion colors have ΔE≈5.5 with a deuteranopia simulation. The lightness difference, not the hue, provides this separation.

amber.$description:
This scale supplies pale backgrounds for comments and dark foregrounds for warnings. Light steps use hues approximately 74–78° (wheat), rather than pure yellow at approximately 90°. At low saturation, 90° yellow can appear olive or khaki. The warmer hues make the light tints appear wheat or cream.

Steps 100–300 have chroma approximately 0.011–0.045, consistent with the other scales. These values keep the comment background close to neutral. At this chroma level, the approximately 78° hue gives the comment background its warm appearance. A higher chroma value is not necessary.

The hue changes monotonically from approximately 78° at the light end to approximately 72° at the dark end. The total change is approximately 6°. Steps 400–900 provide gold foregrounds for warnings and terminals.

blue.$description: This blue scale supplies information, links, functions, documentation backgrounds, and modified lines (diff.change). The light steps supply doc.50 for documentation and quotations. They also supply change.100 for changed lines and changeText.200 for changed words. Documentation and diffs do not occur in the same buffer in this design.

cyan.$description: This cyan scale supplies the terminal cyan foreground at step 600. It also supplies search backgrounds: cyan.300 for all matches and cyan.400 for the current match. These roles use different lightness ranges of a hue that has no other role.

violet.$description: This blue-violet scale supplies constants at step 700 and selection backgrounds at steps 100 and 300. selection.match uses step 100. selection.primary uses step 300. The roles use different buffers and different lightness values.

plum.$description: This red-violet scale supplies the terminal magenta color.

alert.$description:
This alert color is the only exception to the two chroma ranges. All other foreground steps have a chroma limit of approximately 0.045. One color with higher chroma can attract attention before the user reads the text.

alert.fg has C≈0.14, approximately three times the shared limit. It is a single named foreground color, not a numbered scale step. It does not use the perceptual L* sequence. Use it only for error marks that need attention.

The value #B0454E has L≈0.54 and the same 18° hue as the red scale. It has higher saturation than the other red colors. Its contrast against the base background is 4.97:1 (AA). This supports the sign glyph and curved underline.

The threefold chroma increase and the curved underline provide different signals. Chroma magnitude and shape remain signals for red-green color vision deficiency when hue alone is insufficient. Apply this color to curved underlines (sp), bold sign glyphs, and temporary error lines in :messages or the command line. Use it as a foreground color, not a background.

Diagnostic messages that stay in the buffer use status.error (red.700). This prevents a full message line from using the high-saturation red. Warnings use the amber chroma limit, one level below the error emphasis. Information and hint messages have less emphasis.

semantic.$description:
Layer 2 assigns meaning to the primitive colors. Roles describe surfaces, errors, and strings rather than individual tools. Each value refers to a primitive color, so changes to Layer 1 affect all roles.

Green identifies additions and strings. Red identifies deletions and errors. Blue identifies information, links, functions, documentation backgrounds, and backgrounds for changed lines. Amber identifies comments, TODO markers, and warnings. Violet identifies active selections and matching references. Cyan identifies search results.

Cursor-controlled states use hues different from the content that stays on the screen. Lightness differences distinguish roles whose red-green hue differences can disappear with deuteranopia or protanopia. This includes the lightness sequence for additions, changes, and deletions. It also includes the different violet and blue steps for constants, functions, and links.

The +/− symbols in the diff gutter and the curved error underline provide signals without color. Where these shapes are present, they are the primary signals. The lightness difference is an additional signal.

base.$description: Shared neutral background for the editor, terminal, and Zellij.

raised.$description: Background for panels, bars, floating windows, and the tab bar.

code.$description: Background for inline code and fenced code blocks.

cursorline.$description: Background for the current line. Step gray.200 distinguishes it from the base background.

popup.$description: Background for popup windows and Telescope. One step above the base background distinguishes the window area from its border.

key.$description: Background for the active tab, current mode, and cursor position. The gray background has dark text and less contrast than a black background.

default.$description: Color for split separators, the scrollbar, and borders.

primary.$description: Default foreground for body text. The contrast is approximately 8:1 rather than the previous 10:1.

secondary.$description: Foreground for secondary text and status text.

muted.$description: Foreground for hints, line numbers, and secondary interface text. Comments use comment.fg.

strong.$description: Foreground for backgrounds with the most emphasis, such as the current search match. gray.900 meets AA where text.primary has approximately 3.6:1 contrast.

string.$description: Foreground for string literals and Git additions.

constant.$description: Foreground for constants, numbers, and booleans. violet.700 is darker than the function color (blue.600). The lightness difference supports users with color vision deficiency.

link.$description: Foreground for links and URLs. blue.800 differs in lightness from the constant color (violet.700) for users with color vision deficiency. These roles do not share a buffer.

error.$description: Foreground for errors. This is the darkest red, two steps below the warm mode accent, so the colors differ in lightness.

alert.$description:
This color emphasizes error marks. It is separate from status.error (red.700), which supplies the red foreground for terminals, delta, and Zellij. Apply it only to the curved underline and bold sign glyph. Do not use it as a background.

Diagnostic messages and virtual text use status.error, so only the small marks have high saturation. Warnings use amber with less emphasis. See primitive.alert for the chroma rationale.

fg.$description: Foreground for the curved error underline and bold sign glyph. Diagnostic messages and virtual text use status.error.

mark.$description: Small mark for an unsaved buffer or an active macro recording. Its contrast against the background is at least 3:1. Do not use it as a background.

primary.$description:
The active selection uses violet.300 with contrast approximately 1.5:1 against the base background. Its difference from cursorline (gray.200) is ΔE≈6.9. Its difference from diff.change (blue.100) is ΔE≈10.5, or approximately 10.4 with deuteranopia or protanopia simulations. Low chroma limits the hue difference, so the L* difference provides the separation.

The selection remains distinguishable in a changed line. Dark text has contrast approximately 5.2:1. Selection chroma is 0.045, the foreground limit, rather than the lower background chroma.

secondary.$description: Background for inactive selections and menu selections.

match.$description: Background for matching pairs and references. violet.100 relates to selection.primary. Bracket and reference highlights change with the cursor position.

soft.$description:
All search matches use cyan.300 with contrast approximately 1.55:1 against the base background. The difference from the amber comment background is ΔE≈7.8, or approximately 6.5 with a deuteranopia simulation.

One limitation remains. This color and selection.primary (violet.300) have L≈0.82, with ΔE≈2.2 in a deuteranopia simulation. The design treats this as low severity because the search and selection states are temporary. The current match (cyan.400) remains distinct from the selection with ΔE≈11.3 in that simulation. Dark text has contrast approximately 5.3:1.

active.$description:
The current search match uses cyan.400, one step above search.soft. Its difference from search.soft is ΔE≈11.2. This gives the current match more emphasis than the other matches.

Dark text has contrast approximately 3.6:1, which meets AA for large text only. The change to lower-contrast text reduced this value below AA for normal text. The design accepts this limitation because the current match is temporary and follows the cursor.

fg.$description: Comment foreground. This aliases text.secondary so comments have the same contrast as secondary text.

bg.$description:
The comment background uses amber.200 with contrast approximately 1.30:1 against the base background. Its chroma is approximately 0.017, close to neutral. This gives the background a small contrast difference.

The comment foreground supplies most of the emphasis. comment.fg equals text.secondary, with contrast approximately 6:1. The warm background groups the comment region. No other role uses amber.200. diff.change uses blue.

high.$description: Background for TODO, FIXME, WARNING, and NOTE markers. amber.300 is one step above the comment background (amber.200), which distinguishes markers from adjacent comments.

add.$description: Added lines use a tint with contrast approximately 1.29:1 against the base background. diff.delete is one step darker. See diff.delete for the reason for this difference with color vision deficiency.

addText.$description: This color emphasizes words in added lines (delta plus-emph and Neovim DiffText). It is one step above the line tint, which distinguishes the word from the line. It is lighter than diff.deleteText. This lightness difference separates added and deleted words for users with color vision deficiency.

change.$description:
Changed lines (Neovim DiffChange) use blue.100 with contrast approximately 1.13:1 against the base background. The lightness order is change, add, then delete. Add uses green.200 (L≈0.87). Delete uses red.300 (L≈0.82). The difference between add and change is ΔE≈4.9, or approximately 4.8 with a deuteranopia simulation.

The low contrast represents a modification without an addition or deletion. The changed word uses changeText (blue.200) for more emphasis. This matches the VS Code gutter convention: green for additions, blue for modifications, and red for deletions. Dark text has contrast approximately 7.2:1.

changeText.$description: Changed words (Neovim DiffText) use blue.200, one step above changed lines (blue.100). This matches the add/addText relationship: the line uses step N, and the word uses step N+1. The changed word has contrast approximately 1.30:1 against the base background. Dark text has contrast approximately 6.2:1. Only the changed text receives this emphasis.

delete.$description:
Deleted lines use red.300, one step above diff.add. Their lightness is approximately 0.82, compared with approximately 0.87 for added lines. The colors differ in lightness and chroma. The lightness difference is ΔL≈0.053. Equal scale steps have ΔL≈0.012 and can become difficult to distinguish with color vision deficiency.

Deleted lines have more emphasis and a warmer color than added lines.

deleteText.$description: Deleted words (delta minus-emph) use red.400, one step below diff.addText. Their lightness is approximately 0.71, compared with approximately 0.82 for added words (ΔL≈0.111). This lightness difference separates deleted and added words. The word color is darker than the deleted-line color, so the word remains distinct in its line.

primary.$description: Primary cursor background. Its near-black color distinguishes the cursor from the text background.

terminal.$description:
The ANSI palette serves terminals rather than a single tool. Its colors have less emphasis than the editor accents. ANSI color 15 (bright white) must be lighter than color 7 (white) to keep the ANSI order. Against a light background, a color lighter than the lightest AA-compliant gray cannot meet AA for body text.

bright.white uses gray.500 with contrast 3.4:1 (AA for large text). The design selects this as the best value with the ANSI order constraint. white uses gray.600 with contrast 4.9:1 (AA). This is the lightest permitted color 7 that meets AA.

This limitation affects applications that explicitly use ANSI colors 7 or 15 for body text. The default terminal foreground uses text.primary (gray.800), with contrast approximately 8.1:1. Output that uses the default foreground is not affected.
